questions.stem: Which Group By operation returns, for each group, a nested table of all the rows in that group?
questions.explanation: All Rows keeps each group's full detail as a nested Table, which you can then transform, for example to keep the latest row per customer. The other operations return single values.
questions.takeaway: Need each group's detail rows → All Rows.

questions.stem:
A transactions table has 40 million rows with a TransactionDateTime column. Reports only show sales by day and store.

Which Group By produces the smallest table that still meets the requirement?

options.text: Group by Date (date part only) and StoreID, with Sum of Amount
Group by TransactionDateTime and StoreID, with Sum of Amount
Group by Month and StoreID, with Sum of Amount
Group by StoreID only, with All Rows

questions.explanation: Grouping by the date part (not the date-time) and StoreID gives one row per store per day, the grain reports use. Grouping by date-time keeps every timestamp; grouping by month loses daily detail.
questions.takeaway: Aggregate to exactly the grain the reports need.

questions.stem:
You group a Customers query by City and count rows. The exhibit shows the result.

What should you do so each city appears once?

image.alt: Group By result showing separate rows for Paris, PARIS and paris, plus Lyon.

options.text: Standardise City's casing before the Group By step

questions.explanation: Like other Power Query comparisons, Group By is case-sensitive, so Paris and PARIS form separate groups. Standardise the casing (and trim spaces) before grouping.
questions.takeaway: Group By is case-sensitive; clean text first.

questions.stem:
You build a Product dimension by removing duplicates from a flat sales query. You need a whole-number surrogate key, starting at 1, for each product row.

What should you add?

image.alt: Product query after Removed Duplicates and Added Index, with a new ProductKey column numbered 1, 2, 3.

questions.explanation: Add Column > Index Column > From 1 numbers the rows 1, 2, 3 and so on, which works as a surrogate key once the table holds one row per product. A conditional column applies rules, not numbering.
questions.takeaway: Surrogate key in Power Query → Index column from 1.

questions.stem:
A flat AllSales query holds sales and product columns together. You need a Product dimension that automatically picks up any future cleaning steps added to AllSales.

How should you create it?

options.text: Duplicate AllSales, keep the product columns, remove duplicates
Reference AllSales, keep the product columns, remove duplicates
Create a calculated table with DAX

questions.explanation: Reference starts the new query from the output of AllSales, so later changes to AllSales flow into it. Keep the product columns and remove duplicates. Duplicate copies the steps once, so later fixes wouldn't reach it.
questions.takeaway: Build a dimension from a staging query → Reference, not Duplicate.

questions.stem:
Create a Product dimension from the AllSales query so that it stays in sync with AllSales.

Select the actions you should perform and arrange them in order.

items.text: Right-click AllSales and select Reference
Choose Columns: ProductID, ProductName, Category
Select ProductID and Remove Duplicates
Rename the query Product
Right-click AllSales and select Duplicate
Append AllSales to the new query

questions.explanation: Reference AllSales, keep only the product columns, remove duplicates on ProductID so there's one row per product, then give the query a clear name. Duplicating would break the link to AllSales; appending would add rows, not remove them.
questions.takeaway: Reference → choose columns → remove duplicates → rename.

questions.stem:
AllSales now only feeds the Product, Customer and Sales queries built from it.

What should you change on AllSales to avoid loading the same data twice?

options.text: Turn off Include in report refresh

questions.explanation: Turn off Enable load on AllSales. It stays in Power Query as a staging query, the queries that reference it still refresh, and the model only holds the star schema tables.
questions.takeaway: Staging queries → Enable load off.

questions.stem:
A Holidays table loaded from a static file never changes. You want it to stay in the model but skip it during refresh to save time.

What should you change?

options.text: Delete the query after the first load
Mark it as a date table
Turn off Include in report refresh

questions.explanation: Include in report refresh controls whether a loaded query is refreshed; turning it off keeps the existing data in the model. Turning off Enable load would remove the table from the model entirely.
questions.takeaway: Keep in model, skip refreshing → clear Include in report refresh.

questions.stem:
The exhibit shows Query Dependencies. You add a step to AllSales that renames Product Name to ProductName.

Which queries can be affected?

image.alt: Query dependencies: an Excel workbook feeds AllSales (a staging query that isn't loaded), which feeds Product, Customer and Sales, all loaded to the model.

questions.explanation: Product, Customer and Sales all reference AllSales, so any change to its output flows into all three (and could break steps that use the old name). The source file itself isn't changed by Power Query.
questions.takeaway: A change to a referenced query flows to everything downstream.

questions.stem:
The source table regularly gains new columns that reports don't need. The model must not grow when that happens.

Which step should you use?
questions.explanation: Choose Columns (Remove Other Columns) lists the columns to keep, so new source columns are excluded automatically. Remove Columns lists the columns to drop, so any new column passes through and loads.
questions.takeaway: Lock the column list → Choose Columns / Remove Other Columns.

questions.stem:
Only rows with Status = Finished are used in reports. The source is SQL Server, and the query later adds a non-folding step.

Where should you filter on Status?

options.text: As the last step of the query
Early in the query, before the non-folding step

questions.explanation: Filter as early as possible, before any step that breaks folding, so the filter becomes part of the SQL and unwanted rows never leave the server. Filtering after a non-folding step forces Power Query to download every row first; a report filter still loads them all.
questions.takeaway: Filter early, before non-folding steps.

questions.stem:
The Order table has 100 million rows. During development you want to work with a small sample in Power BI Desktop, then publish with the full data, editing as little as possible.

What should you do?

options.text: Copy 1,000 rows into an Excel file and connect to that
Use a parameter in a Keep Top Rows or filter step, and change it in the service after publishing
Use DirectQuery in Desktop and Import in the service
Turn off Enable load during development

questions.explanation: Add a parameter (for example RowLimit) used in a Keep Top Rows step, or in a filter, while developing; after publishing, change the parameter in the semantic model settings so the service loads everything. Editing queries before every publish is error-prone.
questions.takeaway: Dev sample → a parameter controlling rows, changed in the service after publishing.

questions.stem: What does Close & Apply do in Power Query Editor?

options.text: Closes the editor and loads the query changes into the model
Publishes the report to the service

questions.explanation: Close & Apply closes the editor and applies the query changes, loading the results into the model. Apply alone loads without closing. Neither publishes anything.
questions.takeaway: Close & Apply = load changes into the model.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The exhibit shows a model in Model view.

Which table is the fact table?

image.alt: Model view with Customer, Product and Date each related one-to-many to Orders, which holds CustomerKey, ProductKey, DateKey, Quantity and Amount.

questions.explanation: Orders holds the numeric values you aggregate (Quantity, Amount) and a foreign key to each other table, and it sits on the many side of every relationship. Customer, Product and Date describe those orders, so they're dimensions.
questions.takeaway: Fact = numbers to aggregate + foreign keys, on the many side.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The exhibit shows part of a hospital model. A patient who moves address gets a new row in Patient with new ValidFrom and ValidTo dates, keeping the same MRN (medical record number).

Select the answer that completes each statement.

image.alt: Model view with Patient (PatientKey, MRN, Name, City, ValidFrom, ValidTo) related to Visits (VisitID, PatientKey, DateKey, Charge), and Date related to Visits.

parts.label: The fact table is
The surrogate key in Patient is
Patient is an example of

questions.explanation: Visits records events with a numeric Charge and keys to the dimensions, so it's the fact table. PatientKey is the surrogate key: a meaningless number unique per row, even when one MRN has several historical rows. MRN is the business key from the source system. Keeping history this way is a type 2 slowly changing dimension.
questions.takeaway: Surrogate key = unique per row. Business key = the source system's identifier. Type 2 = history kept as extra rows.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
A modeller says the Sales table's grain is 'one row per order line'.

What does that tell you?

options.text: The table has one row per order
Each row represents one product on one order
The table can't be related to Date

questions.explanation: Grain is the level of detail one row represents. Here each row is one product on one order, so an order with three products has three rows. Totals add up correctly from that level, and you can't analyse below it.
questions.takeaway: Grain = what one row of a fact table represents.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
A fact table contains an InvoiceNumber column. Invoices have no other attributes in the source.

How should you model InvoiceNumber?

options.text: Leave it in the fact table as a degenerate dimension
Create an Invoice dimension table with one row per invoice
Remove it, because facts can't contain text
Move it to the Date table

questions.explanation: An identifier with no attributes of its own can stay in the fact table as a degenerate dimension. A separate table with one column per row of the fact table would add a huge relationship for nothing.
questions.takeaway: Identifier with no attributes → leave it in the fact (degenerate dimension).

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem: Why does Microsoft recommend a star schema over a snowflake schema for Power BI models?

options.text: Fewer relationship hops, simpler DAX and an easier field list, with little storage cost

questions.explanation: Every dimension relates directly to the fact table, so filters travel one relationship, DAX stays simpler, and users see fewer tables. Power BI compresses repeated values well, so the storage saving a snowflake offers barely matters.
questions.takeaway: Star = simpler, faster, friendlier. Flatten snowflakes.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The model has Sales and Returns fact tables. Users want to compare sales and returns by product and month in the same visual.

How should you design the model?

options.text: Relate Sales directly to Returns on ProductKey
Relate both fact tables to the same Product and Date dimensions
Merge Returns into Sales on OrderID

questions.explanation: Relate both fact tables to the same Product and Date dimensions (conformed dimensions). A filter on a product or month then reaches both facts. Relating the two facts directly creates a fact-to-fact relationship that's fragile and usually many-to-many.
questions.takeaway: Several facts → share dimensions; never relate fact to fact.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Customers sometimes move city. Reports must show sales by the city the customer lived in at the time of each sale.

What should the Customer dimension do?

options.text: Store City in the Date table
Delete old customers when they move
Add a new row with a new surrogate key whenever City changes, and link each sale to the row current at the time

questions.explanation: A type 2 slowly changing dimension adds a new row (with a new surrogate key) each time a tracked attribute changes, and each sale is linked to the row that was current when it happened. Overwriting the city (type 1) would move all history to the new city.
questions.takeaway: History 'as it was' → type 2 dimension with a surrogate key per version.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Users need two slicers on the same page, Order Month and Ship Month, and want both to filter every visual at the same time.

How should you model the dates?

options.text: Create a second date table for ship dates, each with its own active relationship

questions.explanation: Only one relationship between two tables can be active, so one Date table can't be filtered by both dates at once. Two date tables (for example a calculated copy named Ship Date) each with an active relationship let both slicers work together. USERELATIONSHIP only switches relationships inside specific measures.
questions.takeaway: Two date roles filtered at the same time → two date tables.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
A single imported table has 60 columns: order details plus customer and product attributes repeated on every row. The model is large and confusing.

What should you do?

options.text: Split it into a fact table and dimension tables related by keys
Create a calculated table for each attribute

questions.explanation: Split it into a star: build Customer and Product dimensions (Reference the source, keep their columns, remove duplicates), keep only keys and numeric columns in the fact, then relate them. Repeated text moves out of the biggest table and the field list becomes clearer.
questions.takeaway: Wide flat table → split into a fact and dimensions.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The exhibit shows Sales related to Product, which is related to Subcategory, which is related to Category.

What should you do to make the model a star schema?

image.alt: Model view showing a chain: Category to Subcategory to Product to Sales, each one-to-many.

options.text: Merge Subcategory and Category into Product and stop loading them
Append Subcategory and Category to Product

questions.explanation: Subcategory and Category are a snowflake hanging off Product. Merge them into Product in Power Query (adding Subcategory and Category columns), turn off load for the two lookups, and keep the single Product to Sales relationship.
questions.takeaway: Snowflake chain → merge the outer tables into the dimension.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The exhibit shows a relationship's properties.

In which direction do filters flow?

image.alt: Edit relationship dialog: Sales ProductKey to Product ProductKey, cardinality Many to one, cross-filter direction Single, relationship active.

options.text: Neither, because the relationship is inactive

questions.explanation: Sales is on the many side (ProductKey repeats) and Product on the one side. With Single cross-filter direction, filters flow from the one side to the many side, so selecting a product filters Sales, but filtering Sales doesn't filter Product.
questions.takeaway: Single direction: one side filters the many side.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
You try to create a many-to-one relationship from Sales[ProductKey] to Product[ProductKey], but Power BI says the cardinality isn't valid because Product[ProductKey] doesn't contain unique values.

What should you do?

options.text: Set the cross-filter direction to Both
Remove the duplicate or blank keys from Product

questions.explanation: The one side must hold each key once. Find and fix the duplicate (or blank) ProductKey rows in Product, usually in Power Query, then create the relationship. Choosing many-to-many would hide a data quality problem in a dimension.
questions.takeaway: 'One' side must be unique and not blank; fix the dimension data.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Customer and CustomerDetails each have exactly one row per CustomerID.

What is usually the best design?

options.text: A one-to-one relationship with Single direction
Merge them into a single Customer table

questions.explanation: A one-to-one relationship is valid, but two tables describing the same entity add a needless hop and split the fields users look for. Merging them into one Customer table is simpler and usually smaller.
questions.takeaway: One-to-one usually means the tables should be merged.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
You change the Sales–Customer relationship to Both. Sales is also related to Product and Date.

What is the main risk?

options.text: Sales can no longer be filtered by Date
Ambiguous filter paths and slower, less predictable results

questions.explanation: Bidirectional filtering can create more than one filter path between tables (ambiguity), slows queries, and can produce unexpected results, which is why Power BI may refuse a second bidirectional relationship. Use it only for a specific need.
questions.takeaway: Bidirectional = risk of ambiguous paths and slower queries.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
A Product slicer must show only products that have sales in the current filter context.

What does Microsoft's guidance recommend instead of a bidirectional relationship?

options.text: A visual-level filter on the slicer where a sales measure is not blank
Turning off Edit interactions on the slicer

questions.explanation: Add a visual-level filter to the slicer, such as [Total Sales] is not blank, so only products with sales appear. Microsoft recommends this over making the relationship bidirectional just for a slicer.
questions.takeaway: Slicer showing only 'used' items → visual-level measure filter, not bidirectional.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Customers can share bank accounts, and each account can have several customers. Transactions relate to Account. Users need to filter transactions by customer.

What should you model?

options.text: Relate Customer directly to Transactions on CustomerName
A bridge table with one row per customer and account pair

questions.explanation: A bridge table (CustomerAccount, one row per customer–account pair) sits between Customer and Account. Customer filters the bridge, and the bridge needs to filter Account, which typically means setting the bridge–Account relationship to Both so the filter reaches Transactions.
questions.takeaway: Many-to-many between dimensions → bridge table.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem: For each statement about relationships, select Yes if it is true.
statements: Only one relationship between the same two tables can be active.
The two related columns must have the same (compatible) data type.
A many-to-many relationship always requires a bridge table.
questions.explanation: Only one relationship between two tables can be active at a time. Related columns must have compatible data types, so a text key can't relate to a number key. Power BI supports many-to-many cardinality directly; a bridge table is a design choice, not a requirement.
questions.takeaway: One active relationship per pair of tables; matching types; many-to-many is native.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The exhibit shows two relationships between Date and Sales. One is drawn as a dashed line.

How can a measure use the dashed relationship?

image.alt: Model view: Date related to Sales twice, a solid line to OrderDate and a dashed line to ShipDate.

options.text: It filters automatically when users choose a ship date
Use CALCULATE with USERELATIONSHIP in the measure

questions.explanation: A dashed line is an inactive relationship. It doesn't filter anything by default, but a measure can activate it for its own calculation with CALCULATE and USERELATIONSHIP.
questions.takeaway: Dashed line = inactive; use it in a measure with USERELATIONSHIP.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit shows a (Blank) product row with sales against it.

What is the most likely cause?

image.alt: Matrix of Sales Amount by Category: Apparel, Bags, Footwear, a (Blank) row with 24,605, and a total.

options.text: Some Sales rows have a ProductKey that doesn't exist in Product
The matrix has Show items with no data turned on

questions.explanation: When fact rows have a key that doesn't exist in the dimension, Power BI assigns them to a blank member so totals still add up. Fix it at the source or add the missing products (or an Unknown member) to the dimension.
questions.takeaway: (Blank) row = fact keys with no matching dimension row.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Your DirectQuery model's Sales[ProductKey] always has a matching Product row, guaranteed by the database. You want faster queries.

Which relationship setting should you enable?

options.text: Apply security filter in both directions

questions.explanation: Assume referential integrity tells Power BI it can use inner joins instead of outer joins when querying the source, which is faster. Only enable it when every fact key really does match, or rows will silently disappear.
questions.takeaway: DirectQuery + guaranteed matches → Assume referential integrity.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
In a composite model, Sales comes from SQL Server through DirectQuery and Targets is imported from Excel. In Model view, their relationship shows bracket-like marks after the cardinality indicators.

What do the marks indicate?

options.text: A limited relationship across source groups

questions.explanation: They mark a limited relationship: the tables come from different source groups (or the relationship is many-to-many), so Power BI can't build the join in advance. It runs the join at query time, and no blank member is added for unmatched keys.
questions.takeaway: Bracket-like marks = limited relationship.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem: Which cross-filter direction does a one-to-one relationship use?
questions.explanation: One-to-one relationships always filter in both directions; you can't make them single-direction.
questions.takeaway: One-to-one = always both directions.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem: Select the cardinality Power BI should use for each pair of key columns.

parts.label: Sales[StoreID] repeats; Store[StoreID] is unique
Employee[EmpID] is unique; Badge[EmpID] is unique
Sales[Category] repeats; Budget[Category] repeats

questions.explanation: Unique on one side and repeated on the other is many-to-one. Unique on both sides is one-to-one. Repeated on both sides is many-to-many.
questions.takeaway: Cardinality comes from whether each side's values are unique.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Every time you import tables, Power BI creates unwanted relationships between columns that happen to be named ID.

What should you change?

options.text: Turn off autodetecting new relationships in the Data Load options

questions.explanation: Under Options > Current File > Data Load, clear the Relationships option to autodetect new relationships after data is loaded. You then create the correct relationships yourself in Model view.
questions.takeaway: Unwanted auto relationships → turn off relationship autodetection in Data Load options.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Budget has one row per category per month (stored as the first day of the month). Date has one row per day.

What is a sound way to relate Budget to Date?

options.text: Relate Budget's first-of-month date to Date[Date], and avoid showing budget below month level
Don't relate Budget; use a slicer for each table

questions.explanation: Relating Budget's first-of-month date to Date[Date] lets month, quarter and year filters reach Budget. Visuals below month level would show the whole month's budget on the 1st, so measures should hide or allocate budget at day level.
questions.takeaway: Monthly facts → relate on a month-level date, and guard against day-level visuals.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
You create a second relationship between Date and Sales, on ShipDate, while the OrderDate relationship already exists.

What state is the new relationship created in?

options.text: Active, and the first becomes inactive

questions.explanation: Because only one relationship between two tables can be active, Power BI creates the second one as inactive (dashed line). You can switch which one is active, but not have both active.
questions.takeaway: Second relationship between the same tables → inactive.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem: What happens when you mark a Date table as a date table?

options.text: Power BI creates a relationship to every fact table
Time intelligence uses this table, and its auto date hierarchy is removed
Every date column in the model is converted to this table

questions.explanation: Power BI validates the date column (unique, no blanks, no gaps) and uses that table for time intelligence. The automatic date hierarchy for that table's date column is removed. Data and relationships aren't changed.
questions.takeaway: Mark as date table = validated column + used for time intelligence.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The company's financial year starts on 1 July. Users need to analyse by fiscal year and fiscal quarter, and drill from one to the other.

What should you do?

options.text: Change every date column to Text
Add fiscal year and quarter columns to the Date table and build a hierarchy

questions.explanation: Add FiscalYear and FiscalQuarter columns to the Date table (calculated from the month), then create a hierarchy FiscalYear → FiscalQuarter → Month. Auto date/time only knows calendar years.
questions.takeaway: Fiscal calendars → fiscal columns + hierarchy in your own Date table.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit lists months alphabetically.

What should you do so they appear in calendar order?

image.alt: Matrix of Sales by Month Name listing April, August, December, February, January, July: alphabetical order.

options.text: Set Month Name's Sort by column to Month Number
Change Month Name to the Date type

questions.explanation: Select Month Name and set Sort by column to Month Number (a column with 1 to 12). Every visual then orders months correctly. Sorting a single visual by another field doesn't fix every visual.
questions.takeaway: Text that has a natural order → Sort by column.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
A table visual shows a column titled Sum of Year with values such as 4,048,104.

What should you change?

image.alt: Table visual with columns Region, Sum of Year and Sales, where Sum of Year shows values like 4,048,104.

options.text: Change Year to Text in every visual
Set Year's Summarization to Don't summarize
Format Year with no thousands separator

questions.explanation: Numeric columns like Year default to Sum. Set the column's Summarization property to Don't summarize in the model, so it's treated as a label in every visual.
questions.takeaway: Numbers that are labels (Year, IDs) → Summarization: Don't summarize.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
A map visual plots Paris in France and Paris in Texas at the same location.

What should you do?

options.text: Set the City column's Summarization to Count
Set geographic data categories and add country or state context, for example a hierarchy

questions.explanation: Give Bing enough context: set data categories (City, State or Province, Country) and use the fields together, for example a hierarchy or a combined 'City, Country' column categorised as a place. A single ambiguous city name can't be placed reliably.
questions.takeaway: Ambiguous place names → data categories + more location context.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Users must drill a map from Country to State to City.

What should you create?
questions.explanation: A hierarchy Country → State → City (with each column's geographic data category set) lets users drill down level by level in the map.
questions.takeaway: Drill path on a map → geographic hierarchy.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
A ProductImage column holds web addresses of product photos. You want the photos to appear in a table visual.

What should you set?
questions.explanation: Setting the column's data category to Image URL tells Power BI to render the address as an image in tables, matrices and slicers. Web URL would show it as a link.
questions.takeaway: Show pictures from URLs → data category Image URL.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Report authors keep using foreign key columns such as Sales[ProductKey] in visuals instead of the Product table's fields.

What should you do?

options.text: Hide the foreign key columns in the fact table
Rename them to Do not use

questions.explanation: Hide the foreign key columns in the fact table. They still drive relationships, but authors only see the dimension fields, which have descriptive names and the right behaviour.
questions.takeaway: Hide fact-table keys; use dimension attributes.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
You want Excel users to look up Product information from this semantic model as an organizational data type.

Select how to configure the Product table as a featured table.

parts.label: Row label
Key column

questions.explanation: Mark Product as a featured table. Its row label is what users see in Excel (ProductName). Its key column uniquely identifies each row (ProductID).
questions.takeaway: Featured table: row label = friendly name; key column = unique ID.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Sales Amount must appear as currency with two decimal places in every visual.

Where is the most efficient place to set this?

options.text: On the column or measure in the model

questions.explanation: Set the format on the column or measure in the model (Column tools or Measure tools). Every visual uses it by default, and you don't repeat the setting per visual.
questions.takeaway: Format once in the model, not per visual.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
You hide 30 unused columns in report view to make the model smaller.

Does this reduce the model's size?

options.text: Yes, hidden columns are not stored
No, hidden columns are still loaded and stored

questions.explanation: Hidden columns are still loaded and stored; hiding only removes them from the field list. To shrink the model, remove the columns in Power Query.
questions.takeaway: Hiding ≠ removing. Remove columns to save space.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Profit Margin % must recalculate correctly for any combination of filters users apply, including totals.

What should you create?
questions.explanation: A measure is evaluated in the current filter context, so it gives the right ratio at every level, including totals. A calculated column computes a value per row at refresh, and summing row-level percentages gives wrong totals.
questions.takeaway: Ratios that respond to filters → measures.

questions.topic: Design and implement a data model
questions.stem:
Users need a slicer of customer age bands (Under 25, 25–44, 45+) based on each customer's age.

What should you create?

options.text: A column in the Customer table

questions.explanation: Slicers, rows and axes need values stored per row, so create a column: a calculated column in Customer, or better, a column added in Power Query. A measure can't be used as a slicer field.
questions.takeaway: Slice or group by it → column. Aggregate it → measure.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Sales has Quantity and UnitPrice columns but no amount column. You need a Revenue measure.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: SUMX goes row by row, multiplies Quantity by UnitPrice for each row, and adds the results. Multiplying two SUMs multiplies the totals, which is wrong whenever there's more than one row.
questions.takeaway: Row-by-row calculation, then total → an X iterator such as SUMX.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Sales has one row per order line, and an order can have several lines. You need the number of orders.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: DISTINCTCOUNT counts each OrderID once, however many lines it has. COUNTROWS counts lines, and COUNT counts non-blank values, which also counts lines.
questions.takeaway: Count of entities in a line-level table → DISTINCTCOUNT of the ID.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A Margin % measure divides profit by revenue. Some products have zero revenue, and the visual shows Infinity or errors.

What should you use?
questions.explanation: DIVIDE returns BLANK (or an alternative value you supply) when the denominator is zero or blank, and it's optimised for this. The / operator returns Infinity or an error. IFERROR works but is slower and hides other errors.
questions.takeaway: Division in measures → DIVIDE.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: Why should you create explicit measures instead of relying on implicit measures (dragging a numeric column into a visual)?

options.text: Explicit measures are stored on every row
Implicit measures are slower to refresh
They're reusable, can hold logic, and are needed for features such as calculation groups

questions.explanation: Explicit measures have one definition reused everywhere, can hold business logic, are required by calculation groups, and are what Analyze in Excel and other tools see. Implicit measures are just default aggregations of a column.
questions.takeaway: Define measures explicitly; reuse them everywhere.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Sales has one row per order line. You need the average order value, meaning the average total per order.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: AVERAGEX over the distinct order IDs calculates each order's total (CALCULATE turns each ID into a filter) and averages those totals. AVERAGE of Amount averages lines, not orders.
questions.takeaway: Average per entity → AVERAGEX over VALUES of the entity's ID.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: An employee is active when TermDate is blank. Which two measures return the number of active employees? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
questions.explanation: Both count rows where TermDate is blank: FILTER with ISBLANK keeps only those rows, and COUNTBLANK counts blank values in the column. COUNT counts non-blank values, which gives terminated employees.
questions.takeaway: 'No end date' = blank → ISBLANK filter or COUNTBLANK.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a calculated column in Stores that shows the store name when Status is Open, and is blank otherwise.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: IF checks the condition per row and returns the name or BLANK(). A calculated column has a row context, so Stores[Status] refers to the current row.
questions.takeaway: Row-by-row condition in a column → IF.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a calculated column that labels each customer's credit limit: Low below 1,000, Medium below 10,000, otherwise High.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: SWITCH ( TRUE (), … ) checks each condition in order and returns the first match, which suits ranges. SWITCH on the column itself only matches exact values.
questions.takeaway: Ranges → SWITCH ( TRUE (), condition, result, … ).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Sales relates many-to-one to Product. You need a calculated column in Sales that shows each sale's product category.

Which function should you use?
questions.explanation: RELATED fetches a value from the one side of a relationship into the current row on the many side. RELATEDTABLE goes the other way, returning the many-side rows for a one-side row.
questions.takeaway: Many side needs a one-side value → RELATED.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a calculated column in Customer that counts each customer's rows in Sales. Customer relates one-to-many to Sales.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: RELATEDTABLE returns the Sales rows related to the current customer (it performs context transition), and COUNTROWS counts them. COUNTROWS(Sales) alone would count every sale for every customer.
questions.takeaway: One side needs to count its many-side rows → COUNTROWS ( RELATEDTABLE ( … ) ).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a Blue Sales measure. When a user selects Red in a Color slicer, Blue Sales must return blank rather than ignoring the slicer. The existing filter context must be kept.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: A plain filter argument in CALCULATE replaces any existing filter on Color, so it would return blue sales even when Red is selected. KEEPFILTERS intersects with the existing filter instead: Red and Blue together leave nothing, so the result is blank.
questions.takeaway: Add a filter without overriding the user's → KEEPFILTERS.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit uses Blue Sales = CALCULATE ( [Sales], Product[Color] = "Blue" ). Blue products sold 400 in total.

What does Blue Sales show in the Red row?

image.alt: Matrix of Sales by Color: Blue 400, Green 250, Red 350, total 1,000, with the Blue Sales column shown as a question mark.

questions.explanation: The filter argument replaces the row's Color filter (Red) with Blue, so every row, including Red and Green, shows the blue total of 400. That's why KEEPFILTERS exists.
questions.takeaway: A CALCULATE filter on a column overrides the existing filter on that column.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need each product's share of total sales across all products, whatever product filters are applied.

Which denominator should you use?
questions.explanation: ALL(Product) removes every filter on the Product table, so the denominator is sales for all products (other tables' filters, like dates, still apply). ALLSELECTED would respect slicer selections.
questions.takeaway: Share of all items regardless of selections → ALL on that dimension.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A matrix lists products under their categories. You need each product's share of its own category's sales.

Which denominator should you use?
questions.explanation: ALLEXCEPT removes all filters on Product except Category, so the denominator is the total for the product's category. ALL(Product) would use all categories.
questions.takeaway: Share of the parent group → ALLEXCEPT, keeping the parent column.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: Which filter is generally preferred in CALCULATE for sales above 1,000, and why?

options.text: `FILTER ( Sales, Sales[Amount] > 1000 )`, because it's always faster
`Sales[Amount] > 1000`, because it filters one column instead of iterating the table
Both are identical in meaning and speed
Neither; filters can't use comparison operators

questions.explanation: A boolean filter on one column is evaluated over just that column's distinct values, which is efficient. FILTER(Sales, …) iterates the whole fact table. Note they're not identical: the boolean form replaces any existing filter on Amount, while FILTER(Sales, …) keeps the current context.
questions.takeaway: Prefer column predicates over FILTER on whole tables.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You write CALCULATE ( [Sales], [Margin %] > 0.2 ) and Power BI rejects it.

How should you rewrite the filter?
questions.explanation: Boolean filter arguments can't reference measures. Use FILTER over the items you want to test, here each product, and evaluate the measure for each: FILTER ( VALUES ( Product[Product] ), [Margin %] > 0.2 ).
questions.takeaway: Filtering by a measure → FILTER over a column's values.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: For each statement about evaluation context, select Yes if it is true.
statements: A calculated column is evaluated with a row context for each row.
A row context automatically filters related tables.
Referencing a measure inside a calculated column triggers context transition.
questions.explanation: Calculated columns are evaluated with a row context for each row. A row context doesn't filter related tables by itself; CALCULATE (or a measure reference, which implies CALCULATE) converts it into a filter context. Measures are evaluated in the filter context of each cell of a visual.
questions.takeaway: Row context ≠ filter context; CALCULATE converts one into the other.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A card's title must read 'Sales for North' when one region is selected, and 'Sales for All regions' otherwise.

Which expression should the title measure use?
questions.explanation: SELECTEDVALUE returns the single value in the current filter context, or the alternate result when there are none or several. VALUES would error with several regions; MAX would return one region even when several are selected.
questions.takeaway: Show the selected item or a fallback → SELECTEDVALUE.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A measure must show a value on product rows of a matrix but stay blank on category subtotal rows and the grand total.

Which function tells you whether the current row is at product level?

image.alt: Matrix of Unit Price by Category and Product: product rows show a price, while the Footwear and Bags subtotals and the grand total show blank. Bags contains only one product, Daypack.

questions.explanation: ISINSCOPE ( Product[Product] ) is TRUE when Product is the level currently being grouped, so IF ( ISINSCOPE ( … ), [Measure] ) blanks subtotals. HASONEVALUE can be TRUE at a subtotal when a category holds only one product.
questions.takeaway: Detect matrix level → ISINSCOPE.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit shows Rank = RANKX ( Product[Product], [Sales] ). Every product shows 1.

How should you fix it?

image.alt: Matrix with Product, Sales and Rank columns where every row, including the total, shows a rank of 1.

questions.explanation: In each row, the filter context contains only that product, so it's ranked against itself. ALL ( Product[Product] ) gives RANKX the full list to compare against: RANKX ( ALL ( Product[Product] ), [Sales] ).
questions.takeaway: RANKX needs the full list → ALL on the ranked column.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need the total sales of the five best-selling products, whatever product filters exist.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: TOPN returns a table of the five products with the highest sales (from ALL products), and CALCULATE uses it as a filter. RANKX returns positions, not a filter table.
questions.takeaway: Total for the top N → CALCULATE with a TOPN table.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
What does this measure return?

`Test = VAR s = [Sales] RETURN CALCULATE ( s, ALL ( 'Date' ) )`

options.text: The same value as [Sales] in the current filter context

questions.explanation: A variable is evaluated once, where it's defined, and then behaves as a constant. CALCULATE can't change its value, so Test returns the same as [Sales] in the current context. To ignore date filters, put [Sales] itself inside CALCULATE.
questions.takeaway: Variables are constants once evaluated; CALCULATE can't change them.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Sales has an active relationship to Date on OrderDate and an inactive one on DeliveryDate.

Which expression returns sales by delivery date?
questions.explanation: USERELATIONSHIP activates the inactive relationship for this calculation and deactivates the active one between the same tables.
questions.takeaway: Use an inactive relationship → USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The Customer to Sales relationship is single-direction. One measure must count customers who bought the products selected in a Product slicer.

What should the measure use?
questions.explanation: CROSSFILTER ( Sales[CustomerKey], Customer[CustomerKey], BOTH ) makes the relationship bidirectional for this measure only, so the product filter flows through Sales to Customer. Making it permanently bidirectional affects every visual.
questions.takeaway: Bidirectional for one measure only → CROSSFILTER.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A Budget table has a Category column but no relationship to Product. You need Budget to respond to a Product[Category] slicer without adding a relationship.

Which expression should you use?

options.text: `CALCULATE ( SUM ( Budget[Amount] ), TREATAS ( VALUES ( Product[Category] ), Budget[Category] ) )`

questions.explanation: TREATAS applies the selected Product categories as a filter on Budget[Category], creating a virtual relationship for this measure.
questions.takeaway: Virtual relationship in a measure → TREATAS.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a calendar year-to-date sales measure. The Date table is marked as a date table.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: TOTALYTD ( [Sales], 'Date'[Date] ) sums sales from 1 January to the last date in the current context. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts dates back a year, and DATESMTD is month to date.
questions.takeaway: Year to date → TOTALYTD (or CALCULATE with DATESYTD).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The financial year ends on 30 June. You need fiscal year-to-date sales.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: TOTALYTD's optional year-end argument sets the fiscal year end, here "6/30", so the year-to-date restarts on 1 July.
questions.takeaway: Fiscal YTD → TOTALYTD with a year-end date.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need last year's sales for the same period as the current filter context.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts the dates in context back exactly one year, whether the context is a day, month or quarter. PREVIOUSYEAR returns the whole previous year.
questions.takeaway: Same period last year → SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit shows Sales and Sales PY (prior year).

What should YoY % show for 2026?

image.alt: Matrix of Year, Sales, Sales PY and YoY %: 2025 shows 1,200, 1,050 and 14.3%; 2026 shows 1,320 and 1,200, with YoY % unknown.

questions.explanation: Year-over-year % = (this year − last year) ÷ last year = (1,320 − 1,200) ÷ 1,200 = 10%. Dividing by this year's sales (9.1%) uses the wrong base.
questions.takeaway: YoY % = DIVIDE ( [Sales] − [Sales PY], [Sales PY] ).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need last year's year-to-date sales, up to the same date last year. [Sales YTD] already exists.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: Shifting the dates back a year with SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and evaluating [Sales YTD] in that context gives last year's year-to-date up to the matching date. PREVIOUSYEAR would return the full previous year.
questions.takeaway: Prior-year YTD → [Sales YTD] evaluated over SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A matrix shows sales by day. For each day, you need sales on the same day one month earlier.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: DATEADD shifts the current dates by one month, so each day maps to the same day last month. PREVIOUSMONTH returns every date of the previous month, giving the whole month's total on every row.
questions.takeaway: Shift the current period → DATEADD. Whole previous period → PREVIOUSMONTH.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a rolling three-month sales total ending on the last date in the current context.

Which filter should CALCULATE use?
questions.explanation: DATESINPERIOD returns the dates from the given end date back three months, giving a rolling window. DATESQTD is calendar quarter to date, which resets every quarter.
questions.takeaway: Rolling window → DATESINPERIOD ( dates, MAX date, −N, unit ).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: Which expression returns month-to-date sales?
questions.explanation: TOTALMTD sums from the first day of the month to the last date in context. TOTALQTD is quarter to date and TOTALYTD is year to date.
questions.takeaway: MTD / QTD / YTD → TOTALMTD / TOTALQTD / TOTALYTD.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A measure uses SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( Sales[OrderDate] ) directly on the fact table. Results are wrong for periods with no sales on some days.

What should you do?

options.text: Use a contiguous Date table, related and marked, and reference its Date column

questions.explanation: Time intelligence functions need a date column with every day present (no gaps), which a fact table's date column rarely has. Use a proper Date table, related to Sales and marked as a date table, and reference 'Date'[Date].
questions.takeaway: Time intelligence → a complete Date table, never the fact table's dates.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A card must always show sales for March 2026, whatever the user selects in date slicers.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: REMOVEFILTERS('Date') clears every date filter (including a slicer on a different Date column), then the two filters select March 2026. Filtering only Year and Month without clearing would still intersect with filters on other Date columns, such as a selected date range.
questions.takeaway: Fixed period regardless of slicers → clear the Date table, then filter.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
An AccountBalances table has one row per account per day that a balance was recorded; not every account has a row every day. A matrix shows months.

Which expression returns each month's closing balance using the last date that has data?

options.text: `CALCULATE ( SUM ( AccountBalances[Balance] ), LASTNONBLANK ( 'Date'[Date], CALCULATE ( SUM ( AccountBalances[Balance] ) ) ) )`

questions.explanation: LASTNONBLANK finds the last date in the period where the balance expression isn't blank, then CALCULATE sums the balances on that date. LASTDATE would use the calendar's last day, which may have no rows, giving blank.
questions.takeaway: Closing balance when the last day may be empty → LASTNONBLANK.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: Accounts = CALCULATE ( DISTINCTCOUNT ( Balances[AccountID] ), LASTDATE ( 'Date'[Date] ) ). For each statement, select Yes if it is true.
statements: In a month row, the measure counts accounts that have a row on the month's last date.
If no balances were recorded on the last day of a month, that month shows blank.
The measure counts every account that had a row at any time during the month.
questions.explanation: LASTDATE returns the last date in the current context, so the measure counts the accounts that have a row on that day. If no rows exist on that exact day (for example a weekend), the result is blank. It does not count every account seen during the period.
questions.takeaway: LASTDATE = last calendar date in context, whether or not it has data.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A Headcount table holds one row per department per month, recording headcount on the last day of the month. A matrix shows quarters and years.

Why is SUM ( Headcount[Employees] ) wrong for a quarter, and what should you use?

image.alt: Matrix where January, February and March headcounts are about 600 each, but the 2026 Q1 row shows 1,812.

options.text: It's correct; quarters should add the months
It counts departments, so use DISTINCTCOUNT
It adds three month-end snapshots; take the value at the period's last date instead
It needs AVERAGE over all days

questions.explanation: Headcount is semi-additive: it adds across departments but not across time. Summing three month-end snapshots triples the headcount. Evaluate the sum on the last date of the period instead, for example CALCULATE ( SUM ( … ), LASTDATE ( 'Date'[Date] ) ).
questions.takeaway: Snapshots add across categories but not over time.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You use a quick measure to build a three-month rolling average of Sales, including the current month.

Select the settings.

parts.label: Period
Periods before
Periods after

questions.explanation: With monthly periods, the current month plus the two before it make three months. Periods after is 0, since future months shouldn't be included.
questions.takeaway: N-period rolling window including the current period → N−1 before, 0 after.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a running total of sales from the first date in the data to the current date in context.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: ALL('Date'[Date]) removes the current date filter, and the condition keeps every date up to the current context's last date, giving a cumulative total. Filtering on MIN would only include dates up to the period's start.
questions.takeaway: Running total → FILTER ( ALL ( dates ), date <= MAX ( date ) ).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A measure returns the change in sales compared with the previous month as a ratio, such as 0.05 for 5% growth.

Which expression should you use?

options.text: `VAR p = CALCULATE ( [Sales], DATEADD ( 'Date'[Date], -1, MONTH ) ) RETURN DIVIDE ( [Sales] - p, p )`

questions.explanation: Get the previous month's sales with DATEADD (or PREVIOUSMONTH at month level), then divide the difference by it. DIVIDE avoids errors when the previous month has no sales.
questions.takeaway: Change ratio = DIVIDE ( current − previous, previous ).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Sales and Forecast both have date columns. You need a calculated date table covering the earliest to the latest date across both tables.

Which expression should you use?

options.text: `CALENDAR ( MIN ( MIN ( Sales[Date] ), MIN ( Forecast[Date] ) ), MAX ( MAX ( Sales[Date] ), MAX ( Forecast[Date] ) ) )`

questions.explanation: MIN and MAX each accept two values, so the inner MIN/MAX find each table's extremes and the outer ones compare them. CALENDAR then returns every date in that range. CALENDARAUTO would scan every date column in the model, not just these two.
questions.takeaway: CALENDAR ( earliest, latest ) across tables → nested MIN/MAX.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a date table with 10 full calendar years, ending with the current year.

Which expression should you use?

options.text: `CALENDAR ( DATE ( YEAR ( TODAY () ) - 10, 1, 1 ), DATE ( YEAR ( TODAY () ), 12, 31 ) )`
`CALENDAR ( DATE ( YEAR ( TODAY () ) - 9, 1, 1 ), DATE ( YEAR ( TODAY () ), 12, 31 ) )`

questions.explanation: Start on 1 January nine years before this year and end on 31 December this year: that's ten full years including the current one. YEAR(TODAY())-10 would give eleven years.
questions.takeaway: N full years including this one → start at YEAR(TODAY()) − (N − 1).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a calculated table named Numbers with every integer from −100 to 100.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: GENERATESERIES ( start, end, increment ) returns a one-column table (named Value) with the sequence. It's also what numeric range parameters use behind the scenes.
questions.takeaway: Sequence of numbers → GENERATESERIES.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need a calculated table with one row per year and a column holding that year's total sales.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: SUMMARIZECOLUMNS groups by the given column and adds named expressions, giving one row per year with its sales.
questions.takeaway: Grouped summary table in DAX → SUMMARIZECOLUMNS.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The exhibit shows two single-column tables. You create ProductList = INTERSECT ( GroupA, GroupB ).

Which rows does ProductList contain?

image.alt: Two lists side by side: GroupA holds Bags, Hats, Shoes; GroupB holds Bags, Shoes, Socks.

questions.explanation: INTERSECT returns the rows of the first table that also appear in the second: Bags and Shoes. UNION would combine both lists; EXCEPT would return GroupA rows that aren't in GroupB (Hats).
questions.takeaway: INTERSECT = in both. EXCEPT = in first only. UNION = combined.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Sales has a ProductKey that sometimes doesn't exist in Product.

What is the difference between VALUES ( Product[Category] ) and DISTINCT ( Product[Category] ) in this model?

options.text: VALUES can include the blank row for unmatched keys; DISTINCT doesn't
VALUES returns a single value, DISTINCT returns a table

questions.explanation: VALUES can include the extra blank row Power BI adds for unmatched keys; DISTINCT doesn't. That's why the two can return different counts when referential integrity is broken.
questions.takeaway: VALUES may include the blank row for unmatched keys; DISTINCT doesn't.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Employee has EmployeeID and ParentEmployeeID (the manager). You need a column that lists each employee's chain of managers up to the CEO.

Which function should you use?
questions.explanation: PATH ( Employee[EmployeeID], Employee[ParentEmployeeID] ) returns a delimited string of IDs from the top of the hierarchy to the employee. PATHITEM and LOOKUPVALUE then extract each level, for example to build Level 1, Level 2 columns for a hierarchy.
questions.takeaway: Parent-child hierarchy → PATH, then PATHITEM per level.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You need the number of product categories that had at least one sale in the selected period.

Which expression should you use?
questions.explanation: DISTINCTCOUNT ( Product[Category] ) alone counts every category in the Product table, because filters on Date don't reach Product. Adding Sales as a filter table restricts Product to the rows that have matching sales in the current context.
questions.takeaway: Count dimension items that have facts → use the fact table as a CALCULATE filter.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A Rates table holds Currency, Date and Rate, with no relationship to Sales. You need a calculated column in Sales that returns the rate for each sale's currency and date.

Which function should you use?
questions.explanation: LOOKUPVALUE returns a value from a table by matching one or more columns to values, no relationship needed: LOOKUPVALUE ( Rates[Rate], Rates[Currency], Sales[Currency], Rates[Date], Sales[Date] ).
questions.takeaway: Look up by matching columns without a relationship → LOOKUPVALUE.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: You create a calculation group named Time Calc. Which expression should its Prior Year calculation item use?
questions.explanation: A calculation item applies to whichever measure is in the visual, referenced through SELECTEDMEASURE (). Writing [Sales] would make every measure return prior-year sales.
questions.takeaway: Calculation items use SELECTEDMEASURE ().

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
After you create a calculation group, report authors can no longer drag a numeric column into a visual to sum it.

Why?

options.text: The model now discourages implicit measures
Numeric columns are converted to text
The relationship to the column's table is removed

questions.explanation: Creating a calculation group turns on Discourage implicit measures, because calculation groups only work with explicit measures. Authors must use measures you define.
questions.takeaway: Calculation groups → implicit measures discouraged; use explicit measures.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
Users want a slicer that switches a line chart between Sales, Profit and Units, all of which are measures.

What should you create?

options.text: A field parameter containing the three measures

questions.explanation: A field parameter can contain measures as well as columns. Put it in the chart's value well and in a slicer, and the user's choice swaps the measure shown.
questions.takeaway: Switch measures in a visual → field parameter of measures.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
You want a running total of Sales across the months shown in one matrix, without adding a new measure to the semantic model.

What should you use?
questions.explanation: Visual calculations are defined on a visual and operate on its data, for example RUNNINGSUM ( [Sales] ). They don't add anything to the model.
questions.takeaway: Calculation for one visual only → visual calculation.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem: In DAX query view, which keyword must a query begin with to return a table?
questions.explanation: DAX queries start with EVALUATE followed by a table expression, for example EVALUATE SUMMARIZECOLUMNS ( 'Date'[Year], "Sales", [Sales] ). DEFINE can come before it to declare query-scoped measures.
questions.takeaway: DAX queries → EVALUATE (optionally after DEFINE).

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit shows Max Price per product, and the total row shows 120 instead of the 270 the finance team expects (the sum of each product's maximum).

How should you write the measure?

image.alt: Matrix of Max Price by Product: Daypack 60, Rain Jacket 90, Trail Shoe 120, and a total of 120.

questions.explanation: In the total row, MAX is evaluated over all products together, so it returns the single highest price. To sum each product's maximum, iterate the products: SUMX ( VALUES ( Product[Product] ), CALCULATE ( MAX ( Sales[Price] ) ) ).
questions.takeaway: Totals are recalculated in their own context; iterate to sum per-item results.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A colleague adds + 0 to every measure so that blanks show as zero. Matrices now list every product, even those with no sales.

Why?

options.text: + 0 turns on Show items with no data
Blanks become 0, so no row is blank and every product is shown
+ 0 converts the measure to a calculated column

questions.explanation: Visuals hide rows where every measure is blank. Adding 0 turns blanks into zeros, so every row of the dimension has a value and appears. It also makes visuals slower. Leave blanks as blank, or handle zeros only where needed.
questions.takeaway: Blank hides rows; zero shows them.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
A single card must show 0 instead of (Blank) when there are no sales. Other visuals should keep blanks.

What should the card's measure use?
questions.explanation: COALESCE ( [Sales], 0 ) returns the first non-blank value, so the card shows 0. Using it only in the card's measure keeps other visuals from listing empty rows.
questions.takeaway: Blank to zero for one visual → COALESCE in a dedicated measure.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit uses % of Category = DIVIDE ( [Sales], CALCULATE ( [Sales], ALLEXCEPT ( Product, Product[Category] ) ) ).

What does it show for Trail Shoe?

image.alt: Matrix of Sales by Category and Product: Footwear 500 (Trail Shoe 300, Sandal 200 at 40%), Bags 300 (Daypack 300), total 800. Trail Shoe's percentage is unknown.

questions.explanation: The denominator keeps only the Category filter, so for Trail Shoe it's Footwear's total, 500. Trail Shoe's 300 ÷ 500 = 60%. Dividing by the grand total (800) would give 37.5%.
questions.takeaway: ALLEXCEPT keeps the parent's filter: share of the parent group.

questions.topic: Create model calculations by using DAX
questions.stem:
The matrix in the exhibit uses a running total measure that adds sales from the first date in the data up to the last date in each row's context.

What value appears for March?

image.alt: Matrix of Month, Sales and Running Total: January 100 and 100, February 120 and 220, March 90 with the running total unknown.

questions.explanation: A running total adds every earlier month to the current one: 100 + 120 + 90 = 310. 90 is March alone, and 210 would stop at February.
questions.takeaway: Running total = everything up to and including the current period.

questions.stem:
The exhibit shows Performance Analyzer after you refresh a report page.

Select the answer that completes each statement.

image.alt: Performance Analyzer: the matrix takes 4,470 ms (DAX query 4,120, visual display 310, other 40); the card takes 3,937 ms (DAX query 25, display 12, other 3,900); the slicer takes 96 ms.

parts.label: The visual with the slowest DAX query is
The visual that spends most of its time waiting is
Your first optimisation step should be to
options: copy and analyse the matrix's query

questions.explanation: The matrix spends 4,120 ms in its DAX query, so its measures or model are the bottleneck. The card's own query and display are tiny; its 3,900 ms of Other is time spent waiting, mostly for other visuals. The sensible first step is to copy the matrix's query and analyse it (for example in DAX query view or DAX Studio).
questions.takeaway: DAX query = model/measure work. Visual display = rendering. Other = waiting.

questions.stem:
Performance Analyzer shows that a matrix's DAX query is slow. You want to run that exact query on its own and try changes to the measure.

What should you do?

options.text: Export the visual's data to Excel
Use Copy query, then run it in DAX query view

questions.explanation: Copy query in Performance Analyzer copies the DAX the visual sent. Paste it into DAX query view (or DAX Studio) to run it, inspect the result and test faster versions of the measure.
questions.takeaway: Investigate a slow visual → Copy query → DAX query view.

questions.stem:
The exhibit shows the largest columns in an imported Sales table.

Which change will shrink the model most without affecting reports, which never use transaction-level IDs?

image.alt: Table of Sales column sizes: TransactionGUID 48 million distinct values and 1,412.6 MB (71.8%), SaleDateTime 402.3 MB, Amount 96.1 MB, ProductKey 22.7 MB, Region 0.4 MB.

questions.explanation: TransactionGUID is unique on every row, so it barely compresses and takes most of the table's memory. Removing it (in Power Query) gives the largest saving. Low-cardinality columns such as Region are already tiny.
questions.takeaway: Unused high-cardinality columns (GUIDs, IDs, timestamps) are the biggest wins to remove.

questions.stem:
Product's key is a 12-character text code such as PRD-00045821, used in a relationship to a 50-million-row Sales table.

What change usually improves compression and relationship performance?

options.text: Use an integer surrogate key for the relationship
Add a prefix to every key

questions.explanation: Replacing a text key with an integer surrogate key (for example an index column) makes the key smaller to store and faster to join. Keep the text code as an attribute in Product if users need it.
questions.takeaway: Relationship keys → whole-number surrogate keys.

questions.stem:
You need a ProfitBand column in Sales. You can build it as a DAX calculated column or as a column added in Power Query.

Which does Microsoft's guidance generally prefer, and why?

options.text: A calculated column, because it's always faster
A Power Query column, because it usually compresses better
Neither; use a measure for slicing

questions.explanation: Columns added in Power Query are loaded like source columns and usually compress better. Calculated columns are computed after loading and can compress less efficiently. Use DAX calculated columns when the logic genuinely needs the model (for example RELATED across tables).
questions.takeaway: Prefer Power Query columns over DAX calculated columns where possible.

questions.stem:
A Temperature column holds values with eight decimal places, such as 21.47382915, although reports show one decimal.

What should you do to reduce the model size?

options.text: Round the values to one decimal place in Power Query
Format the column to one decimal place

questions.explanation: Rounding to the precision reports actually use (here one decimal) collapses millions of near-unique values into a few hundred distinct ones, which compress far better. Formatting only changes how values look.
questions.takeaway: Round numbers to the precision you need to cut cardinality.

questions.stem:
The Sales source holds 12 years of history, but reports only cover the current year and the previous three years.

What should you do?

options.text: Add a report-level filter on Year
Hide old years with a slicer
Use a calculated table for recent years
Filter the query to the last four years

questions.explanation: Filter the query to the required years (ideally in a step that folds to the source, or with an incremental refresh archive period) so older rows never load. Report filters still load and store every row.
questions.takeaway: Don't load rows nobody reports on.

questions.stem:
A model has 14 date columns across its tables, and Auto date/time is turned on.

How does this affect the model?

options.text: It has no effect on size
It creates one shared hidden date table
It converts the columns to Text

questions.explanation: Auto date/time creates a hidden date table for each date column, here 14, each spanning that column's full years. Turning it off and using one proper Date table removes them.
questions.takeaway: Auto date/time = one hidden table per date column.

questions.stem:
A DirectQuery Sales table holds 3 billion rows. Most visuals show totals by month and product, which are slow.

What should you implement?

options.text: An imported aggregation table configured with Manage aggregations
A calculated column for each month

questions.explanation: An imported aggregation table summarised by month and product answers those visuals from memory. Configure it with Manage aggregations so Power BI uses it automatically, and set related dimensions to Dual. Detailed queries still go to the DirectQuery table.
questions.takeaway: Big DirectQuery fact + summary visuals → imported aggregation table.

questions.stem:
An aggregation table summarises Sales by month and product. A user opens a visual showing sales by day.

What happens?

options.text: The query falls back to the detailed table
The visual shows monthly values on each day

questions.explanation: The aggregation can't answer day-level questions, so Power BI falls back to the detailed table (through DirectQuery). The user still gets correct results, just more slowly.
questions.takeaway: Queries finer than the aggregation's grain fall back to the detail table.

questions.stem:
A report page has 35 visuals and loads slowly, although each DAX query is fast.

What does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: Reduce the visuals on the page and move detail to drillthrough pages or tooltips

questions.explanation: Each visual sends at least one query and must render, and they queue. Reduce the number of visuals per page: combine visuals, and move detail to drillthrough pages or report page tooltips.
questions.takeaway: Fewer visuals per page; move detail to drillthrough and tooltips.

questions.stem:
A scatter chart with 200,000 points has a long Visual display time in Performance Analyzer.

What should you do?

options.text: Reduce the number of points the visual shows

questions.explanation: Rendering hundreds of thousands of points is slow and unreadable. Reduce the points shown, for example by aggregating to a coarser level or applying a Top N filter. Faster DAX won't fix rendering time.
questions.takeaway: Long visual display time → show fewer data points.

questions.stem: According to Microsoft's DAX guidance, which function should you use to count the rows of a table?
questions.explanation: COUNTROWS counts rows directly, states the intent clearly and doesn't depend on a column's blanks. COUNT ( column ) counts non-blank values, which may differ and reads less clearly.
questions.takeaway: Count rows → COUNTROWS.

questions.stem:
A measure uses IF ( HASONEVALUE ( Region[Region] ), VALUES ( Region[Region] ), "Several" ).

What is a simpler equivalent?
questions.explanation: SELECTEDVALUE ( Region[Region], "Several" ) returns the single value when exactly one exists, otherwise the alternate result. It's shorter and clearer.
questions.takeaway: IF ( HASONEVALUE, VALUES ) → SELECTEDVALUE.

questions.stem:
In a DirectQuery model, slicers on Product and Date are slow because every interaction queries the source. Sales must remain DirectQuery.

What should you change?

options.text: Set Product and Date to Import
Set Product and Date to Dual

questions.explanation: Setting the dimension tables to Dual lets slicer lists be answered from memory while joins to the DirectQuery fact still run at the source. Import would create limited relationships with the DirectQuery fact.
questions.takeaway: DirectQuery fact + small dimensions → Dual dimensions.

questions.stem:
Nightly refresh of a 400-million-row Import table takes four hours, although only recent rows change.

What should you configure?
questions.explanation: Incremental refresh partitions the table by date and refreshes only the recent window, keeping older partitions as they are. Refresh time drops dramatically.
questions.takeaway: Slow full refresh of mostly unchanged history → incremental refresh.

questions.stem:
You want to check the model against a rule set of design best practices, such as unused columns, bidirectional relationships and missing formats.

What should you use?

options.text: Best Practice Analyzer in Tabular Editor

questions.explanation: The Best Practice Analyzer in Tabular Editor runs a set of rules over the model and lists violations. Performance Analyzer times visuals; VertiPaq Analyzer reports sizes.
questions.takeaway: Design rule checks → Best Practice Analyzer.

questions.stem:
You need to see which tables and columns take up the most memory in an Import model.

What should you use?
questions.explanation: VertiPaq Analyzer (available in DAX Studio) reports the size and cardinality of every table and column, showing exactly where memory goes. Performance Analyzer only times report visuals.
questions.takeaway: Where's the memory? → VertiPaq Analyzer (DAX Studio).

questions.stem:
The exhibit shows a model with a many-to-many, bidirectional relationship between Sales and Budget. Visuals that use both tables are slow.

What should you change first?

image.alt: Model view where Sales and Budget are related directly on Category, many-to-many, with a bidirectional arrow.

options.text: Relate Sales and Budget to shared dimensions and remove the direct relationship

questions.explanation: Fact-to-fact, many-to-many, bidirectional relationships are expensive and can be ambiguous. Relate both facts to shared dimensions (Product, Date) with single-direction one-to-many relationships, and remove the direct link.
questions.takeaway: Avoid fact-to-fact and bidirectional many-to-many links; share dimensions.

questions.stem:
You create a calculated table SalesCopy = Sales to use in another part of the report. Sales has 80 million rows.

What is the effect?

options.text: No effect; calculated tables aren't stored
It roughly doubles the memory used by that data

questions.explanation: A calculated table is materialised and stored, so SalesCopy roughly doubles the memory used by Sales. Copying small tables (like Date for a role-playing dimension) is fine; copying a large fact usually isn't.
questions.takeaway: Calculated tables are stored in full; don't copy large facts.

questions.stem: For each statement about model size, select Yes if it is true.
statements: Adding measures doesn't increase the stored size of the model.
Calculated columns increase the stored size of the model.
Hiding a column removes its data from the model.
questions.explanation: Measures are formulas evaluated at query time and store no data. Calculated columns and tables are computed at refresh and stored. Hidden columns are still loaded and stored.
questions.takeaway: Measures: no storage. Calculated columns/tables and hidden columns: stored.

questions.stem:
You need regional managers to see only their own region's data. A static role per region is acceptable.

Select the actions you should perform and arrange them in order.

items.text: In Power BI Desktop, create a role per region in Manage roles
Add a filter such as [Region] = "North" to the Region table in each role
Test each role with View as
Publish, then add each region's security group to its role in the Power BI service
Add the managers to the workspace as Contributors
Turn on Assume referential integrity

questions.explanation: Create roles and their DAX filters in Desktop, test them with View as, publish, then add members (ideally security groups) to each role on the semantic model's Security page. Workspace Contributors would bypass RLS.
questions.takeaway: Create roles → test → publish → assign members.

questions.stem:
